content.text:
Both problems traced. Here's what I found and what I changed.

## 1. Identity swaps — diagnosis only, as you asked

**The tracker has no signal at the two moments it needs one.** `FighterTracker` matches on IoU + centroid distance alone, and [`_assign`](ai/models/FighterTracker.py:126) has **no maximum-cost gate** — only the Hungarian padding cells carry the `1e6` sentinel, so a detection anywhere in the frame always matches *some* slot rather than letting the slot coast. Nothing in `ai/` detects a shot boundary at all.

I measured against your own `corner_swap` label spans — those are ground truth and need no re-run. Fight 54 has 8 spans (6–35 s each, created this morning), fight 52 has 5 (1.7–8.7 s). Against a 5000-frame random control, window ±6 frames:

| | fight 54 | fight 52 |
|---|---|---|
| span **starts** at a big box jump (camera switch) | 4/8 · chance 1.5 | 0/5 |
| span **starts** at high inter-fighter overlap (clinch) | 2/8 | median IoU 0.73 vs control 0.00 |
| span **ends** at high overlap | 4/7 | — |

So both entry points are real, and your "after camera cuts" read matches fight 54 specifically. Small n (5 and 8 spans), so treat it as directional.

**Why they persist until the next cut** is the more useful half. `assign_corners` is the only thing that can repair a tracker swap, and it owns a single *global* slot→corner bijection — it cannot represent "slots are crossed from this cut to the next", only flip the whole fight and flip back. The run log shows it doing exactly that, 444–813 confirmed flips per fight.

And its hysteresis barrier is mis-scaled. `CORNER_HYSTERESIS_WEIGHT` (0.5) is charged per detection whose label flips; a swap always flips both, so the barrier is 1.0. But with no glove tape visible, `_tape_distance_term` returns exactly 0.5 for both corners and cancels — leaving the torso histogram, which can move the two-detection total by at most 0.4 × 2 = **0.8 < 1.0**. A swap is mathematically uncorrectable without visible tape. Meanwhile the single-detection branch charges the barrier only once (0.5), so a one-sided observation faces a *lower* bar than both fighters seen together.

Fight 54 didn't even get that far — the log says `appearance path skipped (ambiguous tape (both slots read blue))`, so the static legacy map ran and no swap was corrected at all. That is the fight you're labelling.

One caution for whenever you pick this up: a global HSV-histogram cut detector is the wrong instrument. Mine found only 29 cuts in 47k frames of fight 54, because broadcast MMA cuts between cameras pointed at the same cage barely move the global histogram. The geometric signal — both boxes jumping at once — is the one that matters anyway.

Written to memory as `tracker-swaps-at-cuts-and-clinches` and `corner-hysteresis-cannot-fix-swaps`.

## 2. Hands outside the box — fixed

Cause is [`box_smoothing`](ai/video_processing/fighter_tracking/box_smoothing.py)'s median(5) + Savitzky-Golay(13) over `(cx, cy, w, h)`. A punch is a 2–4 frame excursion in `w`; the median prefilter exists to delete excursions that short. It cannot tell a punch from the wild box it was built to reject.

Measured on fight 52: a confident wrist landed outside the stored box on **10.2% of frames**, mean 35px, p90 83px. Fast wrists (top decile — mid-strike) were outside 5.9–7.1% of the time versus 1.7% for slow ones. Running the XL pose model over sample windows, the raw box clips too (4.9% vs 8.6% stored), so smoothing roughly doubles it but isn't the only source — which is why I fixed it with a floor rather than by retuning the filter.

Added a fourth pass: the smoothed box is unioned with the frame's own confident keypoint hull, wrists and ankles padded by `BOX_EXTREMITY_PAD_RATIO` (0.20) of fighter scale, since the model marks the wrist bone and not the front of the glove. The hull rather than the raw box, because the wild-box failure is a *box* failure — the skeleton still describes one person. Two guards: the hull is rejected above 6× fighter scale (`BOX_HULL_MAX_SCALE_RATIO`, ~0.9% of hulls, all scattered-joint pose failures), and it's rejected when the skeleton doesn't belong to the box (below).

Replaying the new logic over stored rows predicts: every confident wrist inside its box (1354→0 and 1548→0), median box area ×1.00 and ×1.03, p99 ×1.27. Takes effect on the next pipeline run.

## One thing I found on the way

0.6–0.8% of stored rows have one fighter's box around the *other's* skeleton. The median filter repairs a 1–2 frame identity swap in the box series while the keypoints — which nothing smooths — keep the swapped values. Fight 52 frames 57302–57303 is a clean example: corner 1's shoulder x goes 1245 → 68 → 630 → 1242 while its box sits still. The module docstring currently claims this cannot happen. I guarded the new floor against it but did not repair it — there's a task chip queued for that, since keypoints are the training signal and a mislabelled skeleton is worse than a missing one.

"""Test the motion-blur hypothesis straight off the footage, no pipeline.

For each arm on each frame: elbow speed (normalised by fighter scale) is the
independent variable — the elbow sits nearer the rotation centre, moves slower
and blurs less, and is detected on frames where the wrist is not, so binning on
it can't be circular the way binning on wrist speed would be.

Dependent variables:
  - wrist keypoint confidence, and whether it clears KEYPOINT_MIN_CONFIDENCE
  - sharpness of the hand crop, as variance-of-Laplacian relative to the same
    fighter's torso crop in the SAME frame (cancels global focus, exposure and
    compression, leaving the hand's own blur)
  - whether the RAW pose box contains the wrist, and whether it contains the
    hand position implied by continuing the forearm past the elbow
"""
import os, sys, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import cv2, numpy as np
from ultralytics import YOLO
sys.path.insert(0, "/Users/filip.culig/Developer/fight-ai/ai")
from models.geometry import get_fighter_scale

VIDEO   = "fight_videos/DRAGOJEVICvsHONDA_3.mp4"
WINDOWS = [(20000, 20450), (27400, 27850), (44200, 44650)]
CONF    = 0.4
DEV     = "mps"

model = YOLO("yolo26x-pose.pt")
cap   = cv2.VideoCapture(VIDEO)

def sharpness(gray, cx, cy, half):
    x1, y1 = max(0, int(cx-half)), max(0, int(cy-half))
    x2, y2 = min(gray.shape[1], int(cx+half)), min(gray.shape[0], int(cy+half))
    if x2-x1 < 6 or y2-y1 < 6: return None
    return float(cv2.Laplacian(gray[y1:y2, x1:x2], cv2.CV_64F).var())

    ix1,iy1=max(a[0],b[0]),max(a[1],b[1]); ix2,iy2=min(a[2],b[2]),min(a[3],b[3])
    inter=max(0,ix2-ix1)*max(0,iy2-iy1)
    ua=(a[2]-a[0])*(a[3]-a[1])+(b[2]-b[0])*(b[3]-b[1])-inter
    return inter/ua if ua>0 else 0.0

    cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_POS_FRAMES, lo-1)
    prev = None
    for fnum in range(lo, hi+1):
        ok, im = cap.read()

        res = model(im, verbose=False, device=DEV)[0]
        if res.boxes is None or len(res.boxes) == 0 or res.keypoints is None:
            prev = None; continue

        kps   = res.keypoints.data.cpu().numpy()
        order = np.argsort(-res.boxes.conf.cpu().numpy())[:3]   # 3 biggest people

        gray  = cv2.cvtColor(im, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

            for box, kp in cur:

                for pbox, pkp in prev:
                    s = iou(box, pbox)
                    if s > best: best, bi = s, pkp

                    px = kp[elbow][0] + (kp[elbow][0] - kp[shoulder][0])
                    py = kp[elbow][1] + (kp[elbow][1] - kp[shoulder][1])
                    pin = bool(box[0] <= px <= box[2] and box[1] <= py <= box[3])

                    half = 0.22 * scale
                    hx, hy = (kp[wrist][0], kp[wrist][1]) if wc >= CONF else (px, py)
                    sh = sharpness(gray, hx, hy, half)
                    tx = (kp[5][0]+kp[6][0]+kp[11][0]+kp[12][0])/4
                    ty = (kp[5][1]+kp[6][1]+kp[11][1]+kp[12][1])/4
                    st = sharpness(gray, tx, ty, half)

                    recs.append((sp, wc, win, pin, ratio))

                    if len(samples) < 4000:

                        x2,y2 = min(im.shape[1],int(hx+half*1.6)), min(im.shape[0],int(hy+half*1.6))
                        if x2-x1 > 20 and y2-y1 > 20:
                            samples.append((sp, wc, fnum, im[y1:y2, x1:x2].copy()))
        prev = cur

      f"{'(÷ torso)':>15} {'(when found)':>14} {'outside box':>13}")

   gradient ALONG the direction of travel and preserves it across. So the ratio
   (gradient energy along motion) / (across motion) falls below 1 when the hand
   is smeared, and stays near 1 for a sharp hand. Unlike variance-of-Laplacian
   this is not confounded by how textured the background behind the hand is.

2. Does losing the wrist cost us the BOX?  Calibrate the forearm-extrapolation

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import cv2, numpy as np
from ultralytics import YOLO
sys.path.insert(0, "/Users/filip.culig/Developer/fight-ai/ai")
from models.geometry import get_fighter_scale

VIDEO   = "fight_videos/DRAGOJEVICvsHONDA_3.mp4"

CONF, DEV = 0.4, "mps"
model = YOLO("yolo26x-pose.pt"); cap = cv2.VideoCapture(VIDEO)

def anisotropy(gray, cx, cy, half, ux, uy):
    """(gradient energy along motion) / (across motion) in the crop."""
    x1,y1 = max(0,int(cx-half)), max(0,int(cy-half))
    x2,y2 = min(gray.shape[1],int(cx+half)), min(gray.shape[0],int(cy+half))
    if x2-x1 < 8 or y2-y1 < 8: return None
    p  = gray[y1:y2, x1:x2].astype(np.float32)
    gx = cv2.Sobel(p, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
    gy = cv2.Sobel(p, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
    along  = float(np.mean((gx*ux + gy*uy) ** 2))
    across = float(np.mean((gx*(-uy) + gy*ux) ** 2))
    return along/across if across > 1e-6 else None

    ix1,iy1=max(a[0],b[0]),max(a[1],b[1]); ix2,iy2=min(a[2],b[2]),min(a[3],b[3])

    ua=(a[2]-a[0])*(a[3]-a[1])+(b[2]-b[0])*(b[3]-b[1])-inter
    return inter/ua if ua>0 else 0.0

for lo, hi in WINDOWS:
    cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_POS_FRAMES, lo-1); prev = None

        if r.boxes is None or len(r.boxes)==0 or r.keypoints is None:

        if prev is not None:
            for box, kp in cur:
                best, bi = 0.3, None
                for pbox, pkp in prev:
                    s = iou(box, pbox)
                    if s > best: best, bi = s, pkp
                if bi is None: continue

                    wc = float(kp[w][2])
                    px = kp[e][0] + (kp[e][0]-kp[sh][0]); py = kp[e][1] + (kp[e][1]-kp[sh][1])

          f"{(wc[m]<CONF).mean():10.1%} {np.median(aa) if aa.size else np.nan:19.2f} "

content.text:
You're right about the blur — I can see it and measure it. But it isn't what clips the rectangle. I ran the XL pose model straight over the footage (3 × 450-frame windows of DRAGOJEVICvsHONDA_3, 4,842 arm-observations), binning on **elbow** speed rather than wrist speed so the measurement can't be circular — the elbow sits nearer the rotation centre, blurs less, and is still detected on frames where the wrist isn't.

| elbow speed (scales/frame) | n | wrist lost (conf<0.4) | blur: gradient along ÷ across | wrist inside **raw** box |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00–0.02 | 969 | 10.9% | 0.96 | 98.8% |
| 0.02–0.05 | 1838 | 11.4% | 0.95 | 99.1% |
| 0.05–0.10 | 1337 | 10.3% | 0.91 | 98.2% |
| 0.10–0.20 | 492 | 20.1% | 0.90 | 99.5% |
| 0.20–0.40 | 146 | 26.0% | 0.93 | 99.1% |
| 0.40+ | 60 | 25.0% | 0.88 | 100.0% |

**Your half is confirmed.** On the fastest frames the pose model loses the wrist outright about a quarter of the time versus 11% at rest, and mean wrist confidence falls 0.83 → 0.63. The blur measure is directional — motion blur destroys image gradient *along* the direction of travel and preserves it across, and that ratio drops from 0.96 to 0.88 as the arm speeds up. The contact sheet shows it plainly. (I first tried plain variance-of-Laplacian and threw it out: it *rose* with speed, because a hand swinging out against the cage has more background texture behind it than one resting on the torso. Confounded, not informative.)

**But the box doesn't shrink with the blur.** The raw pose box contains the wrist 98–100% of the time in *every* speed bin — flat, no trend. That's the crux. The person box is drawn around the whole silhouette, and the blur streak is part of that silhouette, so a smeared hand costs you the *skeleton*, not the box.

The clipping is downstream of that. Across all of fight 52, a confident wrist (≥0.5) sat outside the **stored** box on 2.5% of cases versus roughly 1% for the raw box on this sample — smoothing roughly doubles it — and 10.2% of frames had *some* confident keypoint outside the stored box. Those wrists were confidently detected, so they can't be blur cases by construction.

So the two effects are separate, and the fix I made targets the right one: the skeleton floor fires on frames where the keypoint exists and the median filter cropped it. It does nothing on the ~26% blur frames — but on those there's no keypoint to draw anyway and the box is already correct.

Where the blur genuinely costs you is strike detection, not the rectangle. That's already handled deliberately: `ai/CLAUDE.md` notes the velocity baseline holds through the blur frames rather than being divided by the frame gap, so the displacement spans the smear. Your observation is a known, compensated property there.

I added this measurement to the [box_smoothing docstring](ai/video_processing/fighter_tracking/box_smoothing.py) so the next person who asks "isn't it just the footage?" gets the answer without re-deriving it.

One housekeeping note: Postgres was down — OrbStack starts, reports the container, then the daemon socket disappears within a few seconds. I worked around it by measuring from the video, but you'll want to sort that before the next pipeline run.

Mechanism: the median prefilter (`_median`, BOX_MEDIAN_WINDOW_SECS = 0.1 → 5 frames @ 50fps) exists to reject a short, large excursion in the box series. content.text:
Done. The data pushed me away from the repair I'd have guessed at.

## What the measurement changed

I checked the shape of the mismatch population before picking a fix, and the assumption in the brief — that these are two-fighter identity swaps — turns out to describe only a sliver of it:

- **It's overwhelmingly one-sided.** Only 23 of fight 52's 562 mismatched frames, and 14 of fight 54's 460, have *both* rows mismatched. A clean tracker swap crosses both slots, so exchanging the two slots' labels would have addressed about **4%** of the problem. That option is out.
- Displacements run marginal to gross: median 0.15 box diagonals outside, p90 0.65, max 3.65.
- Runs are short — 80% and 93% last 1–2 frames, exactly what a 5-frame median absorbs.

## The repair

Discard the filtered box on those frames rather than try to reconstruct identity. **The observed box is guaranteed to hold its own skeleton** — they're two outputs of one pose detection — so falling back to it restores the pairing by construction, for every cause, without the module having to diagnose which one applied.

New pass 4 (`_skeleton_drift`), running *before* the skeleton floor so the floor always acts on a box that belongs to its keypoints. `det["bbox_xyxy"]` is still the observed value at that point in the loop, so the fallback needs no snapshot. `BOX_SKELETON_DRIFT_RATIO = 0.05` box diagonals, set below the body of the measured distribution while ignoring cases where the torso centre is a few pixels past an otherwise-correct edge.

This also **subsumes `_same_person`**, which is now removed. That helper skipped the floor on mismatched pairs; reverting first means the pair is always consistent, so the floor no longer needs a guard — and the pathological case I'd seen (a box stretched 22× across both fighters) can't arise.

Two things it deliberately doesn't do, both documented in the module: it doesn't repair identity — a row afterwards holds one person's box and that same person's skeleton, still under the wrong slot id — and reverting makes the box **jump on the overlay again**, so the tracker's error is visible to a labeller instead of hidden behind a plausible-looking box. Root cause stays upstream.

The drift check and the median prefilter aren't in tension: a box that engulfs both fighters still *contains* its own skeleton, so it fails no drift test and the median goes on rejecting it.

## Verification

**End-to-end replay** of detection → tracking → smoothing over real frames 57250–57360, old logic vs new — this reproduces your worked example exactly (slot 1 box at x≈1216–1280 with its shoulder at x=68, drift 3.65 diagonals):

| | rows off their own skeleton | worst drift |
|---|---|---|
| old | 22 / 205 | 3.65 diagonals |
| new | **0 / 205** | 0.05 |

At frame 57303 the new output puts slot 0's box at x 1217–1280 with its shoulder at 1242 — box and skeleton together, and the swap now showing as a box jump.

**Synthetic test** reproducing the mechanism in isolation: with the check disabled, the box sits at x 55–135 while the shoulder is at 680 (drift 1.88); with it on, drift 0.00. The punch-floor regression still passes with zero spurious reverts on a clean track.

**DB replay** over all five fights sizes the blast radius: 0.56% of fight 52's rows and 0.43% of fight 54's would revert, everything left below threshold within 0.05 diagonals. Fights 31/42/44 sit at 0.03–0.08% — consistent with smoothing being the cause, though I noted in the docstring it isn't proof, since those predate the XL-pose box and had keypoints IoU-matched to boxes, forcing overlap by construction.

The docstring's false claim is gone, replaced with what actually holds: the pairing is something this module has to actively preserve, not something it gets for free.

Changed: [box_smoothing.py](ai/video_processing/fighter_tracking/box_smoothing.py), [constants.py](ai/models/constants.py). Not yet re-run, so the DB still holds the old rows. One note — Postgres was down again when I started; OrbStack needed a manual start.
Are there any better model that I could potentially use? Or YOLO ones are the best?

You're already on YOLO's largest pose variant, so there's no more headroom within that line. Since this pipeline is offline/batch rather than real-time, you can trade the speed YOLO buys you for accuracy — RTMPose and ViTPose both post better COCO keypoint AP than YOLO-pose, with RTMPose-x being the more practical swap and ViTPose-Huge the ceiling but noticeably slower.

That said, given what we just measured — wrist confidence collapsing specifically on a moving, gloved hand — I'd guess the bigger lever isn't a better COCO backbone at all. Gloves are out-of-distribution for any model trained on COCO's bare-hand data, so a model fine-tuned on boxing/MMA footage would likely close more of that gap than swapping architectures. Want me to look into what's actually available for that (pretrained combat-sports pose models, or what fine-tuning yolo26x-pose on your own footage would take)?
would ViTPose work for "live" video streaming?

Not really — ViTPose is a two-stage top-down model (needs a separate person detector first, then a transformer pass per detected person), which makes it noticeably slower than YOLO-pose even in its smallest variant. ViTPose-B can get close to real-time on a strong GPU for just a couple of people, but it wasn't built for that and you'd be fighting the architecture the whole way.

If live is genuinely the target, RTMPose is the better fit — it was explicitly designed for real-time multi-person pose and reportedly holds most of ViTPose's accuracy at a fraction of the latency, with CPU-viable variants too.

One thing worth flagging: this pipeline is currently offline/batch — `main.py` processes recorded video files start to finish, not a live feed. Swapping toward a "live" model would be a different deployment shape, not a drop-in replacement. Is that actually the direction you're considering, or was this more of a general question?
